title: SARS-CoV-2 Vaccination and Attenuation of Breakthrough Infection Severity: A Systematic Global Review and Meta-analysis.

analysis.scope_and_question: This review investigates the effectiveness of SARS-CoV-2 vaccines in reducing the severity of breakthrough infections, focusing on hospitalization and symptomatic infection outcomes. The central question is whether vaccination attenuates disease severity among those who become infected despite immunization.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a systematic global analysis and meta-analysis of observational studies. It includes 37 studies with 184 VE pairs, using multilevel meta-analysis and metaregression to pool estimates and assess effect modifiers. The methodology involves computing relative VE (rVE) against hospitalization versus symptomatic infection for matched VE pairs.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The pooled relative VE against hospitalization was 51% (95% CI: 39%, 60%) for broadly defined symptomatic infection and 19% (95% CI: 12%, 25%) for medically attended symptomatic infection, indicating that vaccination significantly reduces the risk of progression to hospitalization. The attenuation of severity was sustained over time and did not differ significantly by vaccine platform, though it was lower in older adults aged ≥60 years.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The evidence is limited by small sample sizes, potential selection bias, and inconsistent findings. Substantial heterogeneity was noted, necessitating a focus on stratified and adjusted analyses. There is also variability in attenuation based on the definition of symptomatic infection and the variant period, with weaker attenuation observed for Omicron subvariants when broadly defined symptomatic infection was the comparator.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Further research is needed to address the variability in attenuation across different symptomatic-infection definitions and variant periods. Surveillance and diagnostic strategies should consider these factors, and vaccine effectiveness should be monitored in older adults to ensure sustained protection against severe outcomes.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic global review and meta-analysis evaluates the effectiveness of SARS-CoV-2 vaccines in reducing the severity of breakthrough infections. The study includes 184 vaccine effectiveness (VE) pairs from 37 observational studies, analyzing the relative VE against hospitalization and medically attended symptomatic infection. The pooled rVE was 51% and 19%, respectively, indicating significant attenuation of disease severity among vaccinated individuals. However, the evidence is limited by small sample sizes, selection bias, and heterogeneity, with lower attenuation observed in older adults and for Omicron subvariants. The findings suggest that vaccination markedly reduces the risk of progression to hospitalization, with no significant differences by vaccine platform. Research should focus on understanding variability in attenuation across different definitions and variant periods, and surveillance should account for these factors to optimize public health strategies.

title: Immunogenicity and Safety of Coadministration of AS01E-Adjuvanted Respiratory Syncytial Virus Prefusion F Protein Vaccine and a COVID-19 mRNA Vaccine in Adult s Aged ≥50 Years: A Phase 3, Randomized, Noninferiority Trial.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This trial evaluated coadministration of the AS01E-adjuvanted respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) prefusion F protein-based vaccine (adjuvanted RSVPreF3) and an Omicron XBB.1.5-based coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) mRNA vaccine in ≥50-year-olds.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This phase 3, open-label, multicenter trial randomized ≥50-year-olds 1:1 to coadministration (Co-Ad group) or sequential administration approximately 1 month apart (Control group) of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 and the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine.
analysis.methods: Primary objectives were to demonstrate noninferiority of humoral immune responses at 1 month postvaccination in terms of RSV-A, RSV-B, and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) neutralizing titers, with the upper limit of the 95% CI of adjusted geometric mean titer (GMT) group ratios (Control/Co-Ad) ≤1.50.
analysis.main_results: Noninferiority was achieved for RSV-A (GMT ratio: 1.12 [95% CI: .97-1.28]) and RSV-B (GMT ratio: 1.08 [95% CI: .94-1.23]) and marginally missed for SARS-CoV-2 Omicron XBB.1.5 (GMT ratio: 1.31 [95% CI: 1.13-1.51]).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The marginal miss of the noninferiority criterion for SARS-CoV-2 does not suggest clinically relevant interference.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results support the coadministration of these vaccines, which may have implications for vaccine scheduling in older adults.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report specific limitations of the study design.

analysis.summary_en: This phase 3, randomized, noninferiority trial assessed the immunogenicity and safety of coadministering an AS01E-adjuvanted RSV prefusion F protein vaccine and an Omicron XBB.1.5-based mRNA vaccine in adults aged ≥50 years. The study compared coadministration with sequential administration, with primary endpoints focusing on immune responses against RSV-A, RSV-B, and SARS-CoV-2. Noninferiority was achieved for RSV-A and RSV-B, but the SARS-CoV-2 endpoint was marginally missed. Reactogenicity and safety were generally acceptable, with most events being mild-to-moderate and resolving within 3 days. The findings suggest that coadministration of these vaccines is safe and maintains acceptable immune responses, supporting their use in older adults. The study's results do not indicate clinically relevant interference between the vaccines, and the evidence is strong given the design and outcomes.

title: Immunogenicity and Safety of PHH-1V COVID-19 Vaccine as a Heterologous Booster in Adolescents.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to evaluate the immunogenicity and safety of PHH-1V as a heterologous booster in adolescents, building on its demonstrated effectiveness in adults.
analysis.study_design_and_population: HIPRA-HH-3 was a phase IIb, open-label, multicenter, noninferiority trial involving 240 healthy adolescents (≥ 12 to < 18 years) who had previously received BNT162b2 as a prime vaccine.
analysis.methods: Immunogenicity was assessed by measuring neutralizing antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 variants and total binding antibodies in adolescents compared to young adults (≥ 18 to ≤ 25 years) from a previous trial. T-cell responses were evaluated at day 14 post-booster, and antibody durability and adverse events were monitored through day 336.
analysis.main_results: Neutralizing titers against Omicron BA.1, WH1, Beta, and Delta variants, as well as total binding antibodies, were significantly higher in adolescents than in young adults (P < .001). Cross-variant antibody titers remained above baseline through day 336. Adverse events were mostly mild/moderate, with injection-site pain and headache being the most common within 28 days. No serious adverse events were reported.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings demonstrate that PHH-1V as a heterologous booster in adolescents elicits strong immune responses and is safe, supporting its inclusion in adolescent vaccination strategies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results provide evidence for the effectiveness and safety of PHH-1V in adolescents, which can inform vaccination strategies and contribute to broader public health efforts against SARS-CoV-2.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its focus on a specific age group and the absence of data on younger populations or specific risk groups, which may affect generalizability. The evidence is strong, with statistically significant results and a well-defined noninferiority margin.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the immunogenicity and safety of PHH-1V as a heterologous booster in adolescents. The phase IIb, open-label, multicenter trial involved 240 healthy adolescents who had previously received BNT162b2. Immunogenicity was assessed by measuring neutralizing antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 variants and total binding antibodies, comparing adolescents to young adults from a prior trial. T-cell responses were evaluated at day 14 post-booster, and antibody durability and adverse events were monitored through day 336. Results showed significantly higher neutralizing titers against Omicron BA.1, WH1, Beta, and Delta variants in adolescents compared to young adults (P < .001), with cross-variant antibody titers remaining above baseline. Adverse events were mostly mild/moderate, with no serious events reported. The authors concluded that PHH-1V is safe and elicits strong immune responses in adolescents, supporting its use in vaccination strategies. However, they noted the need for further data in younger populations and specific risk groups.

title: Boosting hybrid immunity with intranasal live-attenuated or intramuscular mRNA vaccination prevents SARS-CoV-2 XBB.1.5 transmission

analysis.research_question_and_background: Rapid antigenic evolution of SARS-CoV-2 and waning immunity have reduced antibody-mediated neutralization, enabling breakthrough infections and sustained transmission despite widespread immunity.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study used a Syrian hamster model to investigate the effectiveness of variant-adapted booster vaccines in the context of pre-existing hybrid immunity.
analysis.methods: The study modeled pre-existing hybrid immunity in Syrian hamsters using intramuscular bivalent mRNA vaccination followed by SARS-CoV-2 infection and then administered heterologous intranasal OTS-LAV or intramuscular mRNA XBB.1.5 booster vaccination.
analysis.main_results: Both booster strategies significantly increased XBB.1.5-binding- and neutralizing antibodies systemically and at mucosal sites. All hybrid-immune animals were protected from disease following XBB.1.5 challenge infection, but virus transmission was completely blocked only after booster vaccination and was associated with the absence of infectious virus in nasal samples.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Booster vaccination left SARS-CoV-2 specific T cell frequencies unchanged, highlighting the unique impact of the OTS-LAV vaccine on antibody responses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings support the use of OTS-LAV as a heterologous booster strategy against SARS-CoV-2 and demonstrate that variant-adapted booster vaccination can efficiently limit transmission, a strategy highly desired for tackling emerging respiratory infections.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a Syrian hamster model, which may not fully represent human immune responses. The evidence is strong, as it directly demonstrates the effectiveness of booster vaccination in preventing transmission.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the effectiveness of variant-adapted booster vaccines in preventing SARS-CoV-2 XBB.1.5 transmission in the context of pre-existing hybrid immunity. Using a Syrian hamster model, researchers administered intranasal live-attenuated or intramuscular mRNA vaccines as boosters following initial bivalent mRNA vaccination and SARS-CoV-2 infection. Both booster strategies significantly increased XBB.1.5-binding- and neutralizing antibodies systemically and at mucosal sites, with complete transmission blockage observed only after booster vaccination, associated with the absence of infectious virus in nasal samples. The findings suggest that OTS-LAV vaccines can effectively boost pre-existing immunity and limit transmission, supporting their use as a heterologous booster strategy. However, the study is limited to an animal model, which may not fully reflect human immune responses.

title: Real-World Effectiveness of International Border Health Interventions in Mitigating the Spread of SARS-CoV-2 During the First Years of the COVID-19 Pandemic, 2020-2023: A Systematic Review.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review aimed to evaluate the real-world effectiveness of international border health interventions, specifically travel-related measures, in mitigating the spread of SARS-CoV-2 during the first years of the COVID-19 pandemic (2020-2023). The focus was on the impact of these interventions on cases, hospitalizations, or deaths related to SARS-CoV-2.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review included 37 observational studies that described international travel-related mitigation measures and their effects on SARS-CoV-2 outcomes. Electronic searches were conducted across multiple databases, including Embase (OVID), Global Health (OVID), CINAHL (EBSCOHost), Cochrane Library, Scopus, Medline (OVID), and World Health Organization COVID-19 Global Literature, covering studies published from January 1, 2020, through February 24, 2023. The ROBINS-I tool was used to assess the risk of bias in these studies.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review found that international travel-related measures, such as quarantine, testing, border closures, and vaccination, had a positive effect on reducing the spread of SARS-CoV-2 early in the pandemic. However, the effectiveness of these measures diminished as the virus spread globally.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The studies included in the review had significant biases, with 14 (38%) judged to have serious or critical risk of bias. analysis.summary_en: This systematic review evaluates the real-world effectiveness of international border health interventions, particularly travel-related measures, in mitigating the spread of SARS-CoV-2 during the first years of the COVID-19 pandemic (2020-2023). The review included 37 observational studies, which collectively indicated that these measures had a positive impact early in the pandemic. However, as the virus spread globally, their effectiveness decreased. The studies were heterogeneous in design and outcomes, and 38% had serious or critical biases. The review emphasizes the importance of developing evaluation strategies for such interventions before implementation to improve their effectiveness in future pandemics.

title: Comparative analysis of production and kinetic assay conditions and parameters for SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro): a systematic review

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the challenges in the production and biochemical characterization of SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro), which is crucial for understanding viral replication and developing antiviral drugs.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This systematic review analyzed existing literature on the production and kinetic assay conditions for Mpro, focusing on experimental limitations and strategies for its expression and purification.
analysis.methods: The review involved an extensive bibliographic search to compile and analyze the main challenges, experimental limitations, and strategies for Mpro production and biochemical characterization, including the effects of assay conditions such as buffer composition, pH, and reducing agents.
analysis.main_results: The review revealed large variability in kinetic parameters across studies, which compromises comparisons and the evaluation of inhibitor efficacy.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted these discrepancies as mainly due to experimental limitations, such as low substrate solubility, optical irregularity, and variations in the oligomeric state of Mpro, highlighting the need for standardization in Mpro research.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings contribute to the standardization of approaches for Mpro production and characterization, which is essential for the development of more effective antiviral inhibitors against SARS-CoV-2.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The review is limited by its reliance on existing literature, and the evidence is moderate as it synthesizes findings rather than presenting original data.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review examines the challenges in producing and characterizing the main protease (Mpro) of SARS-CoV-2, emphasizing the variability in kinetic parameters across studies. The review highlights experimental limitations such as low substrate solubility, optical irregularity, and variations in the oligomeric state of Mpro. It discusses strategies for Mpro expression in Escherichia coli and purification, with a focus on obtaining an N-terminal tag-free enzyme. The findings suggest that standardization of methods is necessary to improve the evaluation of inhibitor efficacy. The review provides a critical perspective on the experimental challenges in Mpro research, which can inform future studies on antiviral drug development. However, the evidence is based on existing literature and is considered moderate in strength due to the lack of original data.

title: T-Cell Response After SARS-CoV-2 Vaccination in Patients With Hematological Malignancy.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on T-cell responses to SARS-CoV-2 vaccination in patients with hematological malignancies (HM), particularly those with immunocompromised status. The central question is whether SARS-CoV-2 vaccination can elicit effective cellular immunity in this population, despite poor humoral responses.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a systematic analysis of 87 studies that evaluated vaccine-induced T-cell response rates in HM patients. The studies were selected based on their assessment of T-cell responses, and the review method involved a structured analysis of these studies to determine the overall response rates.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Across HM subtypes, 75%-87% of studies reported T-cell response rates of at least 50%. This suggests that SARS-CoV-2 vaccination can induce significant cellular immunity in HM patients, even those on immunosuppressive therapy.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Active disease was associated with reduced T-cell responses, indicating variability in vaccine effectiveness based on disease status. However, the evidence does not provide detailed mechanisms or long-term data on T-cell persistence.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: These findings support the continuation of SARS-CoV-2 vaccination strategies for HM patients, even when humoral responses are suboptimal. Further research is needed to explore the impact of active disease on T-cell responses and to investigate long-term immunity.

analysis.summary_en: This review evaluates T-cell responses to SARS-CoV-2 vaccination in patients with hematological malignancies (HM), a population known for poor humoral immunity. A systematic analysis of 87 studies found that 75%-87% reported T-cell response rates of at least 50%, suggesting that vaccination can elicit significant cellular immunity. Active disease was linked to reduced T-cell responses, highlighting variability in vaccine effectiveness. The results support ongoing vaccination efforts for HM patients despite suboptimal humoral responses, but further research is needed to understand the long-term implications and mechanisms of T-cell immunity in this group.

title: Aromaticity at spike position 456 affects functional immunogenicity of SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant receptor-binding domain

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand how the F456L substitution in the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant affects vaccine-induced immune responses, particularly focusing on functional immunogenicity of the receptor-binding domain (RBD).
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used a trimeric RBD-HR subunit vaccine platform to investigate the impact of residue 456 on the functional immunogenicity of the RBD in the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant.
analysis.methods: Single-cell RNA sequencing and B-cell receptor (BCR) repertoire analyses were employed to examine how the F456L mutation affects germinal center responses, clonal expansion, and repertoire remodeling of antigen-specific B cells.
analysis.main_results: The F456L substitution significantly reduced neutralizing antibody responses against multiple SARS-CoV-2 variants, while maintaining comparable levels of total antigen-specific IgG. Structural modeling, biolayer interferometry, and calcium flux assays showed that aromatic residues at position 456 enhance effective germline BCR recognition and activation.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings demonstrate that aromaticity at residue 456 is a critical determinant of RBD functional immunogenicity, highlighting how a single amino acid substitution can alter B-cell responses and antibody quality.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results provide insights for improving vaccine antigen design by emphasizing the importance of residue-specific modifications in enhancing neutralizing antibody responses against SARS-CoV-2 variants.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its focus on a specific vaccine platform and does not generalize to all vaccine types. The evidence is strong as it combines structural, functional, and immunological analyses to support its conclusions.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates how the F456L substitution in the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant affects the functional immunogenicity of the receptor-binding domain (RBD). Using a trimeric RBD-HR subunit vaccine platform, the researchers found that the mutation significantly reduces neutralizing antibody responses against multiple variants, despite maintaining comparable levels of total antigen-specific IgG. Single-cell RNA sequencing and B-cell receptor (BCR) repertoire analyses revealed that the F456L mutation weakens germinal center responses, reduces clonal expansion, and impairs B-cell repertoire remodeling. Structural modeling, biolayer interferometry, and calcium flux assays demonstrated that aromatic residues at position 456 promote effective germline BCR recognition and activation. Replacing the non-aromatic leucine with aromatic amino acids like tyrosine or tryptophan restored the neutralizing antibody-eliciting capacity of the antigen. These findings highlight the importance of residue-specific modifications in vaccine design and show how a single amino acid change can impact B-cell responses and antibody quality. The study's evidence is strong, but its conclusions are limited to the specific vaccine platform used.

title: Differences between Canadian parents' attitudes toward routine, influenza, and COVID-19 vaccines for their children, and changes in vaccine hesitancy since the pandemic: A national cross-sectional comparative study.

analysis.scope_and_question: Background Evidence suggests the COVID-19 pandemic had heterogeneous and vaccine-specific effects on parental attitudes toward childhood vaccination.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: Methods In 2025 we conducted a cross-sectional national online survey of parents with children aged 0-17 years using a polling firm. We calculated proportions and 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Results Parents were most confident in the safety of routine vaccines (71.0%, 95%CI 66.5-75.7), compared to influenza (63.7%, 95%CI 59.5-68.1) and COVID-19 (57.9%, 95%CI 53.9-62.1). The majority indicated the pandemic did not change attitudes about routine (60.8%) or influenza (63.7%) vaccination, while more than one-quarter (31.6% and 27.8%) reported that routine and influenza vaccines were more important following the pandemic. Most parents reported positive or neutral impact of the pandemic on perceived importance of routine and influenza vaccines.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Results A decline in vaccine confidence has been noted in some settings, however even studies reporting stable or increased confidence suggest polarized attitudes with stronger pro- and anti-vaccine views emerging concurrently. In 2025, a slightly higher proportion of parents reported low confidence in the safety and effectiveness of routine vaccines (12.7% and 9.2%, respectively), compared to 2021 (8.5% and 5.6%), and 2020 (12.2% and 6.8%).
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: We explored differences between Canadian parents' attitudes toward childhood routine, influenza, and COVID-19 vaccination, and changes in attitudes since the pandemic.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines differences in Canadian parents' attitudes toward routine, influenza, and COVID-19 vaccines for their children, and changes in vaccine hesitancy since the pandemic. The research highlights that parental confidence in routine vaccines remains higher than for influenza and COVID-19 vaccines. While the majority of parents reported no change in attitudes toward routine or influenza vaccination, some indicated increased perceived importance of these vaccines post-pandemic. The study also notes a slight increase in low confidence for routine vaccines in 2025 compared to 2021 and 2020. Overall, the findings suggest polarized attitudes toward vaccination, with stronger pro- and anti-vaccine views emerging concurrently. The study underscores the need for targeted research and public health strategies to address vaccine hesitancy and improve vaccination rates.

title: Supramolecular assembly and membrane anchoring alter variant-induced SARS-CoV-2 Spike conformational dynamics.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate how supramolecular assembly and membrane anchoring influence the conformational dynamics of SARS-CoV-2 Spike proteins, particularly in the context of viral variants, as these factors are often overlooked in soluble, engineered ectodomain studies.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study compared conformational dynamics of SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein in two constructs: soluble recombinant 2P S and full-length S displayed in virus-like particles (VLPs). The research was conducted using computational and experimental methods to analyze the effects of variant mutations on these constructs.
analysis.methods: The study combined cyclic ion mobility mass spectrometry (CIM-MS) for hydrogen deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDXMS) with computational weighted ensemble molecular dynamic (WE-MD) simulations to assess conformational changes in the Spike protein caused by variant mutations.
analysis.main_results: The results showed that membrane anchoring and virion-like assembly significantly reduced global dynamic changes induced by variant mutations. Specifically, D614G mutation decreased dynamics across interprotomer contacts in VLP S, while Omicron BA.1 mutations reversed this decrease in the S1 domain but preserved reduced dynamics near the fusion machinery.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that the supramolecular context of the Spike protein alters the conformational dynamics of variant evolution, which has direct implications for epitope presentation, antibody recognition, and the interpretation of recombinant Spike structural studies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide important insights into how the structural context of the Spike protein affects its dynamics, which can inform the design of more accurate diagnostic tools, vaccine development, and the understanding of immune responses to SARS-CoV-2 variants.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's results are based on computational and experimental methods, which may have limitations in fully capturing the complexity of native virion conformational dynamics. However, the evidence is strong and directly supports the conclusions drawn about the effects of supramolecular context on Spike protein dynamics.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates how supramolecular assembly and membrane anchoring influence the conformational dynamics of SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein, particularly in the context of viral variants. Using a combination of experimental and computational methods, the researchers compared the effects of mutations on two Spike constructs: soluble recombinant 2P S and full-length S displayed in virus-like particles (VLPs). Their results show that the supramolecular context significantly dampens global dynamic changes induced by variants, with D614G reducing interprotomer dynamics and Omicron BA.1 mutations reversing this effect in the S1 domain while preserving reduced dynamics near the fusion machinery. The authors interpret these findings as highlighting the importance of native conformational ensembles in understanding Spike protein behavior, which has implications for epitope presentation, antibody recognition, and structural studies. The study's methods provide strong evidence, though limitations in fully replicating native virion dynamics may affect the generalizability of the results.

title: Differential expression of lung-homing chemokine receptors in severe COVID-19: distinct profiles between Alpha and Omicron.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Severe Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19), caused by Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), is characterized by excessive pulmonary immune cell recruitment mediated by chemokine - chemokine receptor signaling. Variant-specific differences in lung-homing chemokine receptor expression remain insufficiently defined.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective case-control study analyzed Bronchoalveolar Lavage Fluid (BALF) samples from Intensive Care Unit (ICU) admitted patients with severe COVID-19 during the Alpha (hICU-α) and Omicron (hICU-Ο) waves, along with SARS-CoV-2-negative controls.
analysis.methods: Messenger RNA expression of CXCR1, CXCR2, CXCR3, CCR2, and CCR6 was quantified by Real-Time quantitative Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-qPCR). Protein expression of selected receptors was assessed by western blotting in available samples.
analysis.main_results: CXCR1 expression was significantly increased in hICU-α patients compared with controls (p = 0.02) but not in hICU-Ο patients. CXCR2 expression was elevated in both hICU-α and hICU-Ο groups versus controls (p = 0.008 and p = 0.006, respectively) and was higher in hICU-α than hICU-Ο patients (p = 0.009). CXCR3 expression was increased in both COVID-19 groups compared with controls (p = 0.03 and p = 0.001). CCR6 expression was highest in hICU-Ο patients compared with hICU-α and controls (p = 0.04 and p = 0.001). Increased CXCR2 and CXCR3 protein expression was confirmed in hICU-Ο patients.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Severe COVID-19 is associated with variant-specific alterations in lung chemokine receptor expression, highlighting differential immune trafficking patterns during Alpha and Omicron waves.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings may inform the development of targeted therapies and improve understanding of immune responses in different SARS-CoV-2 variants, potentially aiding in the design of more effective treatments for severe cases.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and potential for selection bias, but the evidence is strong due to the use of multiple assays and clear statistical significance in the results.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates variant-specific differences in lung-homing chemokine receptor expression in severe COVID-19 patients during the Alpha and Omicron waves. Using Bronchoalveolar Lavage Fluid (BALF) samples from ICU patients, the researchers quantified mRNA and protein expression levels of CXCR1, CXCR2, CXCR3, CCR2, and CCR6 via RT-qPCR and western blotting. They found that CXCR1 was significantly increased in Alpha patients but not in Omicron patients. CXCR2 and CXCR3 were elevated in both groups compared to controls, with CXCR2 being higher in Alpha patients. CCR6 was highest in Omicron patients. These results suggest that severe COVID-19 is associated with variant-specific changes in chemokine receptor expression, indicating potential differences in immune trafficking patterns. The study's findings may contribute to understanding immune responses to different SARS-CoV-2 variants and could inform future therapeutic strategies. However, the retrospective design and potential for selection bias limit the confidence in the results, though the evidence is supported by clear statistical significance.

title: Online COVID-19 Misinformation and Infodemic Governance During the Peak Pandemic Period: Scoping Review of Social Media Research From 2020 to 2022.

analysis.scope_and_question: Objective This scoping review synthesizes empirical research on online COVID-19 misinformation on social media during the peak pandemic period from February 2020 to October 2022.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: Methods We conducted a PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses)-informed scoping review of empirical studies indexed in PubMed and IEEE Xplore in November 2022 using COVID-19, social media platforms, and misinformation-related terms.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Results Within the included corpus, the literature was concentrated around vaccine-related discourse, public health and social measures-related misinformation, and text-based data from X (X Corp), formerly known as Twitter.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Its distinct contribution is an integrated comparison of conceptual definitions, thematic and platform concentration, the computational research pipeline, and the gap between detection and actionable infodemic governance.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Future infodemiology research should link computational outputs to intervention design, risk communication, fact-checking workflows, platform moderation, multilingual and multimodal analysis, and the evaluation of infodemic governance strategies.

analysis.summary_en: Objective This scoping review synthesizes empirical research on online COVID-19 misinformation on social media during the peak pandemic period from February 2020 to October 2022. Methods We conducted a PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses)-informed scoping review of empirical studies indexed in PubMed and IEEE Xplore in November 2022 using COVID-19, social media platforms, and misinformation-related terms. Results Within the included corpus, the literature was concentrated around vaccine-related discourse, public health and social measures-related misinformation, and text-based data from X (X Corp), formerly known as Twitter. Its distinct contribution is an integrated comparison of conceptual definitions, thematic and platform concentration, the computational research pipeline, and the gap between detection and actionable infodemic governance. Future infodemiology research should link computational outputs to intervention design, risk communication, fact-checking workflows, platform moderation, multilingual and multimodal analysis, and the evaluation of infodemic governance strategies.

title: Identification of broad-spectrum inhibitors for the cryptic binding site of SARS-CoV-2 NSP1 across multiple variants using molecular dynamics simulation

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to identify broad-spectrum inhibitors targeting the cryptic binding site of SARS-CoV-2 NSP1, which is critical for host immune evasion by suppressing host gene expression through interaction with the 40S ribosomal subunit.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study focused on the cryptic binding pocket of SARS-CoV-2 NSP1, examining its interactions with FDA-approved drugs and evaluating their inhibitory potential against various NSP1 mutants.
analysis.methods: FDA-approved drugs were optimized using the PM6 method, then subjected to virtual screening against the NSP1 cryptic binding site with AutoDock. Molecular dynamics simulations were conducted using GROMACSv2023, and binding free energies were estimated via the MM/PBSA method.
analysis.main_results: Sorafenib was identified as a promising allosteric inhibitor through virtual screening. Molecular dynamics simulations showed that sorafenib binding leads to conformational and dynamic changes in NSP1, resulting in protein stabilization.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted these findings as evidence that allosteric targeting of NSP1 could effectively block its functional role in host translation shutdown, offering a novel strategy for antiviral therapeutics.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that targeting NSP1's cryptic binding site with drugs like sorafenib could provide a broad-spectrum approach to combat SARS-CoV-2 variants, potentially informing future antiviral drug development.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to computational methods and does not include experimental validation, which reduces the strength of the evidence to moderate.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the identification of broad-spectrum inhibitors for the cryptic binding site of SARS-CoV-2 NSP1, a key virulence factor involved in host immune evasion. Using molecular dynamics simulations and virtual screening, the authors identified sorafenib as a promising candidate that stabilizes NSP1 even in the presence of mutations. The findings suggest that targeting this site could offer a novel strategy for antiviral therapeutics. However, the study relies solely on computational methods without experimental validation, limiting the strength of the evidence to moderate.

title: Immunization with JN.1 spike protein increases the breadth of binding and neutralizing antibodies in Syrian hamsters in an immune-history dependent manner.

analysis.research_question_and_background: With much of the world exposed to previous variants of SARS-CoV-2, testing of current COVID-19 vaccines in preclinical models should occur in the context of preexisting immunity to the virus.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Here, we evaluated the immunogenicity and efficacy of a JN.1 variant spike (S) protein-based nanoparticle vaccine in Syrian hamsters nine months after three immunizations with Wuhan-1 prototype, prototype + BA.5, or XBB.1.5 variant COVID-19 vaccines.
analysis.methods: Serum was collected prior to and three weeks after the JN.1 immunization to measure antibody responses to different variants of SARS-CoV-2, including JN.1 and KP.2.
analysis.main_results: Three doses of the nanoparticle S protein vaccine induced long-lasting virus neutralizing antibody responses, and neutralization of the JN.1 and KP.2 variants of SARS-CoV-2 was associated with one or more doses of the XBB.1.5 vaccine.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Subsequent immunization with the JN.1 variant vaccine boosted JN.1 and KP.2 specific antibody responses, however, the relative increase in titer was dependent on vaccine history and inversely correlated with JN.1 neutralizing titers prior to boosting.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Following challenge, JN.1-boosted hamsters, regardless of their immune history or increase in JN.1 specific antibody response, were protected against the KP.2 variant with infectious virus titers averaging at or below the limit of detection in all tissues.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The reductions in viral RNA levels correlated with pre-challenge serum antibody titers against KP.2.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the immunogenicity and efficacy of a JN.1 variant spike protein-based nanoparticle vaccine in Syrian hamsters with preexisting immunity from prior vaccinations. The research highlights the importance of evaluating vaccines in the context of existing immunity, as the effectiveness of the JN.1 vaccine was found to be dependent on the prior vaccine history. The study demonstrates that JN.1-boosted hamsters showed protection against the KP.2 variant, with viral titers at or below the limit of detection. The results suggest that boosting with a variant vaccine can enhance immune responses, but the magnitude of this effect varies based on prior exposure. The findings have implications for vaccine development and the understanding of immune responses in the context of evolving viral variants. However, the study is limited to preclinical models and does not provide direct human clinical data.

title: Persistent COVID-19 Symptoms in General Population and Healthcare Workers: Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis.

analysis.scope_and_question: This review investigates the prevalence of persistent symptoms—collectively termed long COVID—in individuals with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2 infection, comparing the general population with healthcare workers.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The authors conducted a systematic review and meta‐analysis following PRISMA guidelines and registered the protocol in PROSPERO (CRD42023460632). Cohort studies with a minimum follow‐up of 12 weeks after SARS‐CoV‐2 infection were eligible. Searches were performed in PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Scielo, and LILACS/BVS, plus gray literature, up to November 2023. Rayyan was used for article selection, and pooled prevalence estimates were calculated in R. Methodological quality was appraised with the Newcastle‐Ottawa Scale.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Across 58 studies comprising 196,863 participants, the pooled prevalence of fatigue was 0.29 (95% CI 0.24–0.36) and dyspnea 0.16 (95% CI 0.12–0.22). Healthcare workers exhibited lower prevalence rates for several persistent symptoms—including fatigue, dyspnea, cough, taste changes, and gastrointestinal symptoms—than the general population.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The analysis was limited by substantial heterogeneity among studies, and most studies were rated only as fair quality, underscoring uncertainty in the pooled estimates.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The supplied evidence does not report specific research or practice implications.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review and meta‐analysis examined the prevalence of long COVID symptoms in the general population and healthcare workers. Using PRISMA guidelines and a PROSPERO‐registered protocol, the authors included cohort studies with at least 12 weeks of follow‐up, identified 58 studies with 196,863 participants, and assessed quality with the Newcastle‐Ottawa Scale. The pooled prevalence of fatigue and dyspnea were 29% and 16%, respectively, with healthcare workers showing lower rates for several symptoms. High heterogeneity and fair study quality limit confidence in these estimates. No explicit research or practice implications were reported in the abstract.

title: Serologic Testing for Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus and SARS-CoV-2 Cross-Reactive Immune Responses, the Netherlands

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate whether cross-reactive SARS-CoV-2-specific antibodies could affect the specificity of MERS-CoV serology, potentially leading to misclassification of infection history.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was conducted in the Netherlands and focused on individuals exposed to SARS-CoV-2, examining their immune responses to MERS-CoV.
analysis.methods: The researchers combined MERS-CoV S1 binding assays with neutralization tests to assess the impact of SARS-CoV-2-induced cross-reactivity on MERS-CoV serology.
analysis.main_results: SARS-CoV-2 exposure induced MERS-CoV antibodies primarily targeting the conserved S2 domain, with occasional neutralizing capacity.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that cross-reactivity between SARS-CoV-2 and MERS-CoV may influence serological testing, but combining S1 binding with neutralization can mitigate this issue.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results highlight the importance of using combined assays to improve the accuracy of MERS-CoV serology in populations with prior SARS-CoV-2 exposure.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to abstract-level evidence, and the generalizability of findings may be constrained by the specific population and testing methods used.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the potential for SARS-CoV-2-induced cross-reactive antibodies to affect the specificity of MERS-CoV serology in the Netherlands. It found that SARS-CoV-2 exposure led to the production of MERS-CoV antibodies primarily targeting the conserved S2 domain, with some neutralizing capacity. The researchers combined MERS-CoV S1 binding assays with neutralization tests to address this cross-reactivity. The study suggests that using combined assays can improve the accuracy of MERS-CoV serology in populations with prior SARS-CoV-2 exposure. However, the findings are based on abstract-level evidence, and the study's generalizability may be limited. The results have implications for improving serological testing methods to avoid misclassification of infection history due to cross-reactivity.

title: Vaccination rates, facilitators and barriers for influenza, pneumococcal and SARS-CoV-2 vaccination among sepsis survivors: a Mid-German Sepsis Cohort survey

analysis.scope_and_question: Sepsis survivors often suffer from chronic immune dysfunction, leading to frequent rehospitalization and recurrent sepsis. Vaccinations are effective in preventing common infections in sepsis survivors. However, vaccination behavior in this vulnerable population remains unknown.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: Prospective interviewer-administered survey performed between 04/2023 and 04/2024 among sepsis survivors in Germany. Participants were recruited from the Mid-German Sepsis Cohort (MSC) 6 to 8 years after initial inclusion. Predictors for the vaccination status of each of the three infections were identified by logistic regression analyses.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Among 174 survivors, vaccination rates against influenza and pneumococci rose from 57.3 to 70.7% and from 31.4 to 60.5% 3 months to 8 years post-sepsis, respectively. A total of 135 patients (77.6%) had full vaccination coverage against SARS-CoV-2 at the time of the survey. Vaccination counselling by a general practitioner increased the odds for vaccination between 5.5-fold (influenza) and 3.2-fold (pneumococci) in the multiple regression analyses. The review of general vaccination status was associated with a 4.7-fold increase of influenza vaccination rates and 3.1-fold increase of SARS-CoV-2 vaccination rates.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: No associations between sociodemographic indicators and the vaccination status against pneumococci and SARS-CoV-2 were found. Among patients with at least one missing vaccination (n = 92), impaired mobility (16.8%), long waiting times in the practice (14.8%) and fear of infection in the practice (14.7%) were the most relevant barriers. There are considerable vaccination gaps in sepsis survivors.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Pro-active vaccination counselling and checks of vaccination status by general practitioners may offer a great potential to increase vaccination rates and thus should be considered as an important element of sepsis aftercare.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores vaccination rates, facilitators, and barriers for influenza, pneumococcal, and SARS-CoV-2 vaccines among sepsis survivors in Germany. A prospective survey of 174 sepsis survivors, conducted between 2023 and 2024, revealed that vaccination rates for influenza and pneumococci increased over time, with 77.6% of participants having full SARS-CoV-2 vaccination coverage. Logistic regression analyses identified higher age and intermediate education as predictors for influenza vaccination, while general practitioner counseling significantly increased vaccination odds. Barriers such as impaired mobility, long waiting times, and fear of infection were reported among those with incomplete vaccination. The study highlights the need for proactive vaccination counseling and status checks in sepsis aftercare to address existing gaps.

title: Mitigation of imprinted antibody responses against COVID-19 in highly vaccinated older adults.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Despite higher clinical risk of severe COVID-19, contemporary data on antibody durability and breadth in older adults receiving multiple COVID-19 booster vaccines remain limited amid ongoing evolution of SARS-CoV-2 Omicron JN.1 descendants and the divergent BA.3.2 saltation variant.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We studied a clinically vulnerable cohort of 43 older adults (median age = 85 years, IQR 75-88, 40% female).
analysis.methods: Using pseudotyped and surrogate virus neutralization-based assays, we demonstrate that JN.1 and KP.2 vaccinations six months apart elicit high-potency neutralization across all studied JN.1-lineage variants but not BA.3.2.2, where titers were 2-3-fold lower.
analysis.main_results: Waning of serum neutralizing activity was modest between vaccine doses, suggesting sustained immunity.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Importantly, the half-life of serum neutralization against Wu-1 (179 days) was substantially longer than JN.1 subvariants (43.7-70.1 days), consistent with Wu-1-specific imprinted responses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Furthermore, BA.3.2.2 neutralizing antibody half-life was prolonged at 107 days, implicating imprinted ancestral variant-targeting antibodies having some activity against BA.3.2.2.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: While absolute neutralization titers remained highest against ancestral Wu-1 due to multiple historical exposures, recall responses after the KP.2 vaccine revealed a shift in immunodominance.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates antibody responses in older adults who received multiple booster vaccines against SARS-CoV-2, focusing on the durability and breadth of immunity against recent variants. The research highlights that despite the clinical vulnerability of this population, biannual, strain-updated booster vaccines can reduce immune imprinting and sustain neutralizing activity against emerging variants. The findings suggest that while ancestral variant-specific antibodies may persist, they do not fully impede responses to newer variants like BA.3.2.2. These results have implications for vaccine strategies in the elderly, emphasizing the need for updated formulations to maintain effective protection. However, the study's abstract-only nature and limited scope may restrict the depth of conclusions that can be drawn.

title: Associations between salivary HHV-6 and long COVID severity in a cross-sectional, case-control analysis.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the relationship between long COVID symptoms and salivary HHV-6 DNA, cortisol, testosterone, and oestradiol levels, building on the background that reactivation of human herpesviruses, particularly EBV, is associated with more severe acute SARS-CoV-2 infection and the development of Long COVID.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A cross-sectional, case-control study was conducted with 45 participants diagnosed with long COVID and 45 age-sex-matched controls.
analysis.methods: Salivary cortisol, testosterone, and oestradiol were measured, and extracted nucleic acid was tested for EBV, HSV 1/2, HCMV, and HHV-6 A/B using multiplex qPCR, and for SARS-CoV-2 and RNaseP using RT-qPCR. Surveys and validated health questionnaires were used to collect demographics, medical history, and symptom profiles.
analysis.main_results: Salivary HHV-6 DNA levels were positively associated with a greater aggregated long COVID propensity score (r = 0.24, 95% CI = 0.02-0.44, p = 0.015, adj. p = 0.030), as well as anxiety (β = 0.69, 95% CI = 0.02-1.36, p = 0.045) and depression (β = 0.24, 95% CI = 0.05-0.42, p = 0.013) scores. analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The observed correlation between salivary HHV-6 DNA and symptom severity suggests HHV-6 may contribute to post-acute disease, though mechanisms remain unclear.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings highlight the potential importance of HHV-6 in long COVID pathophysiology and underscore the need for longitudinal, multi-compartment studies of herpesvirus reactivation in long COVID.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is cross-sectional, limiting causal inference, and the sample size may not be sufficient to capture all potential associations. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the observational nature of the study.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the relationship between long COVID symptoms and salivary HHV-6 DNA, cortisol, testosterone, and oestradiol levels. It enrolled 45 participants with long COVID and 45 age-sex-matched controls in a cross-sectional, case-control design. Salivary cortisol, testosterone, and oestradiol were measured, and nucleic acid was tested for HHV-6 and other herpesviruses using qPCR. The results showed a positive association between salivary HHV-6 DNA levels and a greater aggregated long COVID propensity score, as well as anxiety and depression scores. However, no significant differences were found in EBV or HHV-6 DNA between the groups. The authors suggest that HHV-6 may contribute to post-acute disease, though mechanisms remain unclear. The findings highlight the potential role of HHV-6 in long COVID pathophysiology and emphasize the need for further longitudinal studies. The study's cross-sectional design limits causal inference, and the moderate sample size may affect the strength of the conclusions.

title: Association Between Acute Vulvar Ulcers and Gene-Based COVID-19 Vaccines.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Acute vulvar ulcers have been reported following gene-based COVID-19 vaccinations, though causality remains uncertain.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This observational study analyzed vulvar ulcer cases reported to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) from January 2002 to February 2022.
analysis.methods: Causality was assessed using the Bradford Hill criteria.
analysis.main_results: From 2021 to 2022, the proportion of vulvar ulcers among reported adverse events exceeded the upper control limits for the first time since 2002. Most cases (134/137, 97.8%) were linked to COVID-19 vaccines. Ad26.COV2.S had the highest relative risk (2.72 vs. BNT162b2; 95% CI: 1.17-6.30). For two-dose vaccines, the second dose posed a higher risk (dose 2 vs. dose 1: RR 3.52; 95% CI: 2.06-6.02 for BNT162b2; RR 2.40; 95% CI: 1.82-3.18 for mRNA-1273). Adolescent females aged 12-17 years had the highest risk (RR vs. age 25-39: 4.01; 95% CI: 2.67-6.05), with a 46.0-fold increased risk (95% CI: 11.2-188.9) compared to age-matched females who received HPV vaccines.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Vulvar ulcers were closely associated with COVID-19 vaccination, especially in adolescent females.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest the need for increased surveillance and awareness of vulvar ulcers as a potential adverse event following gene-based COVID-19 vaccination, particularly in adolescent females.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: While findings suggest a potential link, further research is warranted to determine causality.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the association between gene-based COVID-19 vaccines and acute vulvar ulcers. It reports that the proportion of vulvar ulcers among adverse events exceeded control limits in 2021-2022, with most cases linked to vaccines. Ad26.COV2.S showed the highest relative risk, and the second dose of two-dose vaccines posed greater risk. Adolescent females had a significantly higher risk compared to other age groups. The study concludes that vulvar ulcers are closely associated with vaccination, especially in adolescents, but emphasizes the need for further research to confirm causality. The evidence is based on VAERS data and Bradford Hill criteria, with limitations in establishing definitive causality.

title: Time to resolution of Long COVID symptoms and the associated factors among the people infected with SARS-CoV-2 during the 3rd wave of COVID-19 in Zambia: A prospective quantitative study

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate the time to resolution of Long COVID symptoms and the associated factors among individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2 during the 3rd wave of COVID-19 in Zambia.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A prospective quantitative study was conducted over 24 months (September 2021-August 2023) involving a cohort of 303 participants randomly sampled from 7 healthcare facilities in Lusaka and Southern provinces.
analysis.methods: Demographic and clinical data were collected at baseline and monthly intervals from participants’ clinical records and interviews. Survival analysis (Kaplan Meier model) was used to determine the median time to symptom resolution, generate survival curves, and the risk table. A Poisson model was fitted to compute the crude incident rate of recovery, and Cox-Proportional Hazards regression analysis was conducted to assess the association between covariates and time to resolution of symptoms.
analysis.main_results: A total of 236 events occurred during the follow-up period; the crude incidence rate was 1,575.6 events per 1000 person years (95%CI: 1,363.2 - 1,784.4). The median time from diagnosis of Long COVID symptoms to resolution was 6 (IQR: 5-8) months. Vaccination status was significantly associated with the time to resolution of symptoms (aHR= 1.71, 95% CI: 1.02 - 2.86, p=0.04) after adjusting for age, number of children, occupation, pre-existing medical conditions, number of vaccine doses and hospital admission. Other variables did not show statistically significant association with the time to resolution of symptoms (p>0.05).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that vaccination is associated with a shorter time to resolution of Long COVID symptoms. Crude and adjusted hazard ratios, 95% confidence intervals and p-values were computed to support this interpretation.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study provides insights into the resolution of Long COVID symptoms and highlights the potential role of vaccination in influencing recovery time, which can inform public health strategies for managing post-COVID conditions.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The observational design of the study limits the ability to establish causation. A study with an experimental design is needed to confirm the causal relationship between vaccination and symptom resolution.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the time to resolution of Long COVID symptoms and associated factors among individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2 during the 3rd wave of the pandemic in Zambia. Conducted over 24 months, it included 303 participants from seven healthcare facilities. Demographic and clinical data were collected monthly, and survival analysis, Poisson modeling, and Cox-Proportional Hazards regression were used to assess outcomes. The median time to symptom resolution was 6 months, and vaccination status was significantly associated with shorter recovery times (aHR=1.71, 95% CI: 1.02-2.86, p=0.04). Other variables did not show significant associations. The study suggests a potential link between vaccination and symptom resolution but emphasizes the need for experimental designs to confirm causality. These findings may inform public health strategies for managing post-COVID conditions.

title: Pregnancy and iron deficiency anemia are associated with COVID-19 severity: a retrospective cohort study from Gaza.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate the association between pregnancy and iron deficiency anemia (IDA) with the severity of COVID-19, given that pregnancy is recognized as a risk factor for severe disease and IDA may exacerbate this vulnerability through impaired immune function, reduced oxygen transport, and altered coagulation and endothelial function.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective cohort study was conducted at Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza from 2021, involving 271 unvaccinated, otherwise healthy women aged 18-38 with COVID-19. The study stratified participants into pregnant (n = 97) and nonpregnant (n = 174) groups based on IDA status.
analysis.methods: Iron deficiency was assessed using transferrin saturation levels <20% measured during acute infection. Ferritin levels were not available for analysis. A multivariable model was used to evaluate the association between IDA and severity of illness, including critical illness and fatal outcomes.
analysis.main_results: Pregnancy was significantly associated with increased severity of COVID-19, with pregnant women having higher odds of critical illness (OR = 4.61, 95% CI 2.27-9.39, p < 0.001) and death (OR = 5.25, 95% CI 1.91-14.44, p = 0.001) compared with moderate illness. IDA was also associated with higher odds of severe, critical, and fatal illness in both pregnant and nonpregnant women.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that pregnancy and IDA are associated with increased severity of COVID-19, highlighting the potential impact of these factors on disease outcomes in young, otherwise healthy, unvaccinated women.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that monitoring and addressing iron deficiency in pregnant women may be important for improving outcomes in severe cases of COVID-19, particularly in resource-limited settings like Gaza.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study has limitations due to the small number of events, particularly deaths, and the reliance on transferrin saturation alone to assess iron status, which may not distinguish preexisting iron deficiency from inflammation-related changes.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the association between pregnancy and iron deficiency anemia (IDA) with the severity of COVID-19 in a cohort of 271 unvaccinated, otherwise healthy women aged 18-38 in Gaza. The results showed that pregnancy was significantly linked to higher odds of critical illness and death, while IDA was associated with increased severity in both pregnant and nonpregnant women. The authors suggest that these factors may influence disease outcomes, emphasizing the need for targeted surveillance and management. However, the study's small sample size and reliance on transferrin saturation alone to assess iron status limit the strength of the evidence, necessitating caution in interpretation.

title: Integrating Individual-Level Syndromic Surveillance Data Into Infectious Disease Modeling for COVID-19 Forecasting in Sweden: Comparative Modeling Study.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the effect of integrating syndromic surveillance data on short-term COVID-19 forecast accuracy, addressing the need for timely surveillance and accurate forecasting to curb disease transmission and reduce health burden.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This comparative modeling study was conducted in Sweden between March 2 and December 31, 2020, using data from the 1177 health care helpline cross-linked with national registers on testing, hospitalizations, and deaths. The study population included individuals reporting symptoms to the helpline and those who tested positive for COVID-19.
analysis.methods: The researchers developed a novel epidemiological model named SI s I c HRD, incorporating individual-level syndromic surveillance data from the 1177 health care helpline with aggregated data on testing, hospitalizations, and deaths. They used a daily rolling-window approach with a 60-day fitting period to predict confirmed infections, hospitalizations, and deaths over the subsequent 30 days.
analysis.main_results: The SI s I c HRD model achieved a median mean MAPE of 61.6% (IQR 37.6%-79.6%) for confirmed cases, 37.5% (IQR 18.9%-57.5%) for hospitalizations, and 0.65% (IQR 0.3%-1.9%) for deaths. Compared to the model without syndromic surveillance data, the SI s I c HRD model reduced MAPE by an average of 15.7 percentage points for confirmed cases, 8.17 percentage points for hospitalizations, and 1.99 percentage points for deaths.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the results as demonstrating that integrating individual-level syndromic surveillance data with health care helpline data improves the predictive accuracy of severe outcomes such as hospitalizations and deaths, while capturing early signals from symptomatic individuals and distinguishing suspected cases from confirmed infections.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that this framework can enhance the accuracy of short-term forecasts for severe outcomes of COVID-19, supporting public health decision-making during future outbreaks.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's evidence is limited to abstract-only data, and the model's performance was evaluated using mean absolute error and mean absolute percentage error, which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world forecasting. The confidence in these results is moderate.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the effect of integrating syndromic surveillance data from Sweden's 1177 health care helpline into an epidemiological model for predicting short-term COVID-19 outcomes. The novel SI s I c HRD model incorporated data on suspected and confirmed infections, hospitalizations, and deaths, achieving higher predictive accuracy for severe outcomes compared to a model without such data. The model demonstrated improved performance for confirmed cases, hospitalizations, and deaths, with significant reductions in mean absolute percentage error. These results highlight the potential of combining individual-level data with aggregated health data to enhance forecasting accuracy, which could support public health decision-making in future outbreaks. However, the study is based on abstract-only evidence, and the confidence in the findings is moderate due to the limited scope of the data and the absence of detailed statistical analysis.

title: Coronavirus health beliefs and fetal health concerns: associations with preventive health behaviors during COVID-19.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to examine the role of concerns about fetal health in shaping preventive health behaviors (PHB) during the COVID-19 pandemic, addressing a knowledge gap in understanding how health beliefs influence PHB.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic, involving 202 pregnant Israeli women who completed online questionnaires assessing their concerns about fetal health, health beliefs, and adherence to PHB.
analysis.methods: Participants completed online questionnaires assessing concerns about fetal health, health beliefs (perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits, and barriers), and adherence to PHB. Multiple hierarchical regression and mediation analyses were conducted.
analysis.main_results: Concerns about fetal health were positively associated with PHB. Perceived susceptibility and perceived benefits were also positively associated with PHB, whereas perceived barriers were negatively associated; perceived severity was not significant. Mediation analyses indicated that concerns about fetal health fully mediated the association between perceived susceptibility and PHB and partially mediated the associations between perceived severity and perceived benefits and PHB.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that concerns about fetal health play important direct and indirect roles in adhering to PHB during pregnancy, providing new insights into the influence of health beliefs on PHB.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings may guide health services in developing tailored programs during pandemics to enhance PHB among pregnant women.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its cross-sectional design and reliance on self-reported data, which may introduce bias. The sample was specific to pregnant Israeli women, limiting generalizability.

analysis.summary_en: This study examined the role of concerns about fetal health in shaping preventive health behaviors during the COVID-19 pandemic among 202 pregnant Israeli women. It found that concerns about fetal health, perceived susceptibility, and perceived benefits were positively associated with PHB, while perceived barriers were negatively associated. These findings suggest that health services should develop tailored programs to enhance PHB during pandemics.
